title: SMART on FHIR: Authorization for Healthcare Apps
summary: How SMART on FHIR uses OAuth 2.0 to enable secure, delegated access to FHIR data for patient-facing and clinician-facing applications.

objectives.text: Explain what SMART on FHIR is and why it is needed
Distinguish between EHR launch and standalone launch contexts
Describe how SMART scopes control what data an app can access

content_blocks.body:
FHIR defines how health data is structured and exchanged — but it does not define who is allowed to access that data, or how an application proves it is acting on behalf of a patient or clinician. That is the job of SMART on FHIR: Substitutable Medical Applications, Reusable Technologies. Developed at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School beginning in 2010, SMART on FHIR created a standard authorization framework layered on top of FHIR APIs using OAuth 2.0 — the same authorization protocol used by Google, Facebook, and virtually every major web platform.

The core insight of SMART is that health apps should work like apps on a smartphone: a patient should be able to connect an app to their EHR the same way they connect Spotify to their Google account — by granting specific permissions, reviewing what data will be shared, and being able to revoke access at any time. Before SMART, every EHR vendor had proprietary APIs with custom authentication — an app built for Epic would not work with Cerner, and vice versa. SMART created a standardized authorization layer that, in combination with FHIR, makes apps genuinely portable across EHR systems.

ONC's certification rules require that all certified EHR technology implement SMART on FHIR — specifically the SMART App Launch Framework. This mandate means that any app built on SMART can theoretically connect to any certified EHR, giving patients and clinicians a genuine ecosystem of interoperable applications.
content_blocks.heading: The authorization layer that made the app store possible

items.definition: The patient (or clinician) who owns the health data and grants permission to apps to access it on their behalf.
The FHIR server — typically the EHR system — that holds the actual health data and validates access tokens before serving data.
The third-party app requesting access to FHIR data — a patient portal app, a population health tool, a clinical decision support application.
The server that authenticates the user and issues access tokens — often built into the EHR platform alongside the FHIR server.
A short-lived credential issued by the authorization server that the app presents to the FHIR server to prove it has been authorized to access specific data.
A longer-lived credential that allows the app to obtain new access tokens without requiring the user to re-authenticate — used for background/ongoing access.

content_blocks.heading: SMART launch contexts

content_blocks.body: SMART scopes define exactly what data an app can access. The syntax is [context]/[resource].[operation]. For example: patient/Observation.read (read observations for the current patient), user/MedicationRequest.read (read medication requests for any patient the user can access), system/*.read (read all resource types — for backend system access). The EHR's authorization server validates these scopes against user permissions before issuing a token. An app requesting broader scopes than needed is a red flag — users should review requested scopes carefully before granting access.

content_blocks.label: apps in the Epic App Orchard built on SMART on FHIR
content_blocks.context: Epic's app marketplace (App Orchard) has over 400 certified SMART on FHIR applications as of 2024 — a direct result of the standardized authorization layer that SMART provides. Similar ecosystems exist for Oracle/Cerner and other EHR platforms.
